client: I just feel so empty since my brother died. Everyone keeps telling me to "move on" or "find happiness again," but how am I supposed to do that? Even simple things like watching TV or meeting friends just make me feel worse because he's not here to share them with me.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're missing your brother, and how painful it is when people suggest moving on before you're ready. It makes sense that everyday activities feel hollow when you're grieving such an important person in your life. What does "moving on" mean to you, and how does that idea make you feel?

client: The idea of "moving on" makes me feel sick to my stomach. It's like people expect me to just forget about him or stop loving him, and that's never going to happen. Even small things like seeing his favorite snacks at the store make me freeze up because it feels wrong that the world keeps going when he's not here anymore.
therapist: Your love for your brother is so strong, and it's completely understandable that the thought of moving on feels impossible when your bond remains so present in your heart. The world continuing without him must feel like such a painful contrast to the stillness inside you. Would it feel more comforting if we thought about ways to honor your brother rather than "moving on"?

client: Honoring my brother sounds nice in theory, but it also feels overwhelming. I don’t even know where to start, and part of me worries that trying to do something special for him might just make the pain feel sharper. It’s like, how do you honor someone when their absence is still so raw and heavy?
therapist: It's completely understandable that the idea of honoring him feels overwhelming right now - grief makes even simple things feel impossibly hard. The pain is still so fresh that any act of remembrance might indeed amplify the ache of missing him. What if we started by simply noticing when small moments remind you of him, without any pressure to "do" anything about those feelings yet?

client: I appreciate you saying that - it does feel impossible to even think about honoring him right now without breaking down. But the idea of just noticing small moments...I don't know, sometimes those little reminders hurt the most, like when I pass his favorite coffee shop or hear a song he loved. It's like a fresh stab every time.
therapist: Those "fresh stabs" show how alive your connection to him still is - the pain exists because your love does too. Right now, the reminders might feel like wounds, but I wonder if there's any tiny comfort in recognizing that these moments are evidence of how deeply he's woven into the fabric of your world? The coffee shop, the songs - they're threads that still connect you to him, even though it hurts to pull on them right now. Would it feel possible to simply acknowledge those threads when they appear, even if all you can say is "This hurts because I love you"?

client: It’s hard to think of those threads as anything but painful right now. Every time I hear “our” song or walk past that coffee shop, it feels like I’m reliving the loss all over again. I get what you’re saying about acknowledging the love behind the pain, but it doesn’t really make it easier to carry. It just feels like I’m stuck in this loop of hurt.
therapist: It sounds like those reminders are reopening the wound every time, and the love you feel for your brother is currently inseparable from the pain of his absence. Right now, the grief feels like a cycle that keeps pulling you back into that raw place of loss. Would it feel helpful to explore together how we might honor both the love and the pain, perhaps finding ways to let those moments exist without them overwhelming you completely?

client: I want to believe that's possible, but it just feels like the pain swallows up everything else whenever I think about him. Even happy memories just make me miss him more. I'm not sure how to separate the love from the hurt when they feel so tangled together.
therapist: It makes complete sense that the love and pain feel inseparable right now - grief has a way of braiding them together so tightly. The happy memories might be bittersweet now, but they show how much light he brought to your life. What would it feel like to let those memories exist just as they are - both joyful and painful - without trying to untangle them yet?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's just so hard to hold both those feelings at once. When I think about the happy times, the pain of losing him crashes over me like a wave. It makes me want to push all the memories away because they hurt too much. 

Sometimes I wonder if it would be easier to just... not remember at all. But then I feel guilty for even thinking that, because it's like I'm trying to erase him. I don't know how to find a middle ground.
therapist: I hear how torn you feel - wanting to keep your brother close through memories, yet needing relief from the overwhelming pain they bring. That guilt makes so much sense because it comes from the same place as your love - you don't actually want to forget him, you just want the hurt to ease. What if we thought about these waves of grief not as something to push away or drown in, but as something you could gradually learn to float with?

client: I get what you're saying about learning to float with the grief, but it just feels impossible right now. Every time I try to think about him without breaking down, the guilt creeps in that I'm not honoring his memory enough. And the idea of the pain easing almost scares me—like if it hurts less, I'm forgetting him or moving on too fast.
therapist: I hear how deeply conflicted you feel - wanting the pain to ease while fearing that any relief might mean you're letting go of your connection to him. That guilt about "not honoring him enough" shows just how much your love for your brother continues to shape your experience of grief. What if we explored what "enough" looks like to you - might there be ways to honor him that feel authentic to your relationship, rather than measuring up to some impossible standard?

client:
I don't know what "enough" would look like. Every time I try to think about moving forward, it feels like I'm betraying him. Like if I'm not constantly grieving, it means I didn't love him enough when he was here. 

The idea of finding "authentic" ways to honor him makes me anxious - what if I choose wrong? What if the ways I remember him aren't good enough? He deserved so much better than how things ended.
therapist: I hear how much pressure you're putting on yourself to grieve "correctly" - it's clear your brother meant the world to you, and that love makes you want to honor him perfectly. The fear of choosing wrong comes from such a caring place, because you want to reflect how special he was. What if we considered that there's no "wrong" way to remember someone you loved so deeply - that the very worry about doing it "right" already shows how much he matters to you?

client:
I know logically there's no "right" way to grieve, but it feels like if I don't do certain things—like visiting his grave every week or keeping all his belongings—I'm somehow failing him. The guilt creeps in whenever I have a good day or think about moving forward. 

Part of me wants to believe you, but another part keeps insisting that if I really loved him, I'd be stuck in this pain forever. Does that make sense?
therapist: Your struggle makes so much sense - the logical part of you knows there's no "right" way to grieve, but the emotional part feels like moving forward would mean leaving him behind. That guilt about having good days shows just how deeply you care - it's not that you want to be stuck in pain forever, it's that you don't want to lose your connection to him. What if we explored how you might carry him with you into the future, rather than feeling like moving forward means leaving him in the past?
